newsitem.title: UK: Britain's fifth TV channel seeks March 1997 launch.
newsitem.headline: Britain's fifth TV channel seeks March 1997 launch.

text.p: Britain's fifth terrestrial television channel is likely to launch in late March 1997, three months later than planned, Channel 5 chief executive David Elstein said.
"What's been widely rumoured in the trade press is an Easter date -- the last weekend of March -- and I wouldn't demur from that," Elstein told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday.

Elstein, who joined Channel 5 from satellite and cable television broadcaster BSkyB last month, said he had suggested a specific new date to the Independent Television Commission (ITC), instead of a January 1 debut.
The watchdog will discuss the date on Thursday and Elstein hopes that it will be possible to confirm it on Friday.

Channel 5, the third British commercial terrestrial network, said last month it would delay its launch for four to six weeks after it was granted access to an additional frequency that would make it available to as many as 1.8 million extra homes.

The new frequency boosts Channel 5's coverage to more than 80 percent of the country but increases the number of homes which its retuners must visit. Retuners will adjust video recorders to prevent interference from the channel's signal.
Elstein said he had underestimated the number of extra homes which would need retuning when he originally planned for a maximum delay of six weeks.

The granting of the additional frequency meant more than three million extra homes would have to be visited by retuners -- those included in the coverage area for the first time plus many others now facing potential interference.
He believed that Channel 5 would have a maximum of 8,000 retuners working for it at a cost of around 120 million pounds ($190 million).
Channel 5 is a consortium comprising British media groups Pearson and United News & Media plus Luxembourg broadcaster CLT and U.S. investment firm Warburg Pincus.

Elstein said the three-month delay was insignificant when set against a licence running for 10 years. There would be an unexpected financial windfall as it would not now make its first 22 million pounds annual licence payment until January 1998.
"I think the shareholders are feeling pretty bullish about the whole enterprise," he said. The channel aims to break even within three years of its launch.
He hoped to make the channel available via cable and satellite from the start and said the addition of Channel 5 could encourage more viewers to take Sky's satellite package.
"Sky has its own good reasons for wanting to have Channel 5 on satellite. So long as they can find capacity at a price which we can afford, we would certainly want to go down that route."

Channel 5's initial programming budget will be only around 110 million pounds annually -- considerably smaller than that of its four existing terrestrial rivals. But Elstein said he thought that was a "good, solid sum of money" for its plans.

Most outside estimates are for Channel 5 to take a five to six percent share of all viewing and Elstein said that would be a respectable figure to have reached by this time next year. ($1=.6317 Pound)
